Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The two recurrent lesions are located in segments II and III of the left liver, which is the only remnant after the prior right hepatectomy. Resection of both lesions would leave only segment IV as future liver remnant. The structured analysis lacks a quantified FLR ratio (Future Liver Remnant volume) and arterial anatomy, both decisive for determining whether the remaining liver will be sufficient to sustain postoperative function. Because this information is missing, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The need to obtain volumetric data (and, if inadequate, to consider portal vein embolization or alternative local therapies) fulfills the requirement for the “Potentially resectable” category.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging: obtain a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease; perform contrast‑enhanced liver CT or MRI with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR and delineate arterial anatomy, capsular infiltration, and any atypical features.  
- Verify status of the primary colon lesion: if the left‑colon primary has not yet been resected, schedule a curative colectomy (or endoscopic removal if feasible) before liver‑directed therapy.  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to treat micrometastatic disease and potentially downsize the hepatic lesions.  
- Re‑image after systemic therapy and repeat FLR volumetry:  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present) and no capsular invasion, proceed to anatomic left lateral resection (segments II‑III) with negative margins.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization of the left lateral sector to hypertrophy segment IV, followed by repeat volumetry and, if adequate, staged left lateral resection.  
   • If FLR remains inadequate or the lesions are borderline, employ percutaneous ablative techniques (RFA/MWA) as an alternative or adjunct to surgery.  
- Post‑operative management: resume/adapt systemic therapy based on pathological response and multidisciplinary discussion; monitor CEA and imaging surveillance every 3–6 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
- Quantitative FLR ratio/volumetry (Future Liver Remnant adequacy).  
- Detailed arterial anatomy of the left liver (to plan safe resection or embolization).  
- Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to definitively rule out occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Confirmation of whether the primary left‑colon tumor has already been resected.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic relevance).  
- History of prior systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, response).  

These missing elements must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm) occurring in the left lateral section after a prior right hepatectomy, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesions are peripherally located but arise in the only remaining functional liver. Resection is technically feasible but must strictly preserve adequate parenchyma and inflow/outflow. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy, pending volumetric confirmation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative volumetric and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and ensure preservation of sufficient functional parenchyma.
• Assess portal inflow and venous outflow carefully given prior right hepatectomy.

B. Peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (220 ng/mL) and early recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the 2 lesions of segments II and III aiming for R0 margins.
• Avoid any formal left hepatectomy or extended resection.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of segments II and III on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the first hepatectomy.
E. a chest CT scan F. Exact CEA trend prior to detection of recurrence.

Case_Content:

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment

Definitive resectability hinges on two decisive pieces of information that are currently missing: (a) quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) after a right‑sided (segment VIII) resection, and (b) confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease on comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal imaging. Until these data are available, surgery cannot be performed safely, but there is no absolute anatomic or oncologic contraindication.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1️⃣ Complete staging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or osseous metastases that were not reported.

   • Proceed with right‑sided hepatic resection focused on segment VIII, employing vascular control techniques;  
   • If IVC invasion persists, plan for limited IVC resection with primary repair or graft reconstruction, depending on extent.  
- 6️⃣ Post‑operative management: resume/adapt systemic therapy (adjuvant) based on pathological response and margin status; consider surveillance with serial CEA and imaging.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative FLR ratio (Future Liver Remnant compatibility) – essential to determine whether a segment VIII resection is safe after prior left hepatectomy.

These missing items must be obtained before a definitive surgical decision can be made.

Case_Content:
Woman, 55 years old, history of left hepatectomy for synchronous metastases. Surveillance: CEA 560 ng/mL. Liver MRI: multiple lesions in right and left lobes (up to 4.5 cm). RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Diffuse liver recurrence, potentially non-curative.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The MRI demonstrates multiple bilateral lesions up to 4.5 cm after a prior left hepatectomy, indicating a high tumor burden and likely limited future liver remnant (FLR). The structured analysis lacks critical data that directly determine surgical feasibility – specifically the FLR ratio, the exact hepatic segments involved, and the presence of vascular or biliary invasion. Because these missing items are decisive for whether a curative resection can be performed, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” At the same time, there is no definitive information (e.g., proven extra‑hepatic disease or irreversible loss of FLR) that would make the disease “Not resectable.” Therefore the appropriate classification is “Potentially resectable,” pending completion of the missing assessments and possible down‑staging measures.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1. Complete staging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases that were not evaluated on the current MRI.  
- 2. Assess liver functional reserve: calculate the FLR volume on cross‑sectional imaging (CT volumetry or MRI) and compare to the required threshold (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % after prior major resection).  
- 3. Initiate systemic therapy: start a first‑line regimen appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR antibody such as cetuximab or panitumumab) to attempt tumor down‑staging and to treat occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- 4. Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months of chemotherapy: repeat liver MRI (or CT) to assess radiologic response, lesion size, and to re‑measure FLR.  
- 5. If FLR is insufficient but tumor burden has decreased, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
- 6. Surgical planning:  
   • If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows limited disease confined to segments that can be cleared with an extended right hepatectomy (or right trisectionectomy) while preserving an adequate FLR, proceed to curative liver resection, possibly combined with intra‑operative ablation of marginal lesions.  
   • If disease remains diffuse or FLR cannot be rendered adequate, shift to a non‑curative (palliative) approach: continue systemic therapy, consider hepatic arterial infusion or selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) for liver‑dominant disease, and address the primary tumor if symptomatic or still unresected.  
- 7. Throughout, monitor CEA trend; a falling CEA after chemotherapy supports response, whereas persistently high levels may prompt earlier consideration of palliative strategies.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Exact location and resection status of the colorectal primary tumor (needed to decide whether primary resection is required).  
- Number of liver metastases, hepatic segments involved, and presence of vascular or biliary invasion (determine technical resectability).  
- Quantified future liver remnant (FLR) ratio (critical for safety of any repeat hepatectomy).  
- Results of thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- History of prior systemic chemotherapy (to know if the patient is chemotherapy‑naïve or already exposed).  
- Presence of symptoms from the primary tumor (obstruction, perforation, bleeding) that could mandate urgent colorectal surgery.  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right hepatectomy in 2021 for three KRAS mutated metastases. Liver MRI 2025: two new lesions segments IVb and II (2.7 and 3.2 cm).No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 300 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar liver recurrence, sufficient liver volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Resectable upfront  
• Reasoning: The patient has only two metachronous liver lesions (2.7 cm in segment IVb and 3.2 cm in segment II) with no radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT. The structured analysis confirms that the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio is compatible with surgery, indicating that sufficient functional liver will remain after resection. Absence of documented vascular or biliary invasion and the fact that the lesions are confined to segments that can be addressed with limited anatomic or non‑anatomic resections support immediate surgical feasibility.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• 1. Multidisciplinary review confirming KRAS‑mutated disease; obtain full molecular profile of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) if not already known.  
• 2. Initiate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑month FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat micrometastatic disease and to observe tumor biology, given the elevated CEA (300 ng/mL).  
• 3. Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) after chemotherapy to reassess lesion size, vascular contact, and FLR.  
• 4. If imaging confirms that both lesions remain resectable with adequate margins and FLR, proceed to surgery: perform a left lateral segmentectomy (segment II) combined with a limited resection of segment IVb (segmentectomy or wedge) preserving as much non‑tumorous left liver as possible.  
• 5. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of a 6‑month total systemic regimen) should be administered, tailored to KRAS status and any additional molecular findings.  
• 6. Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑4 months during the first 2 years, then every 6 months thereafter.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Primary colorectal tumor details (location, grade, molecular phenotype, and whether it has already been resected) – essential for staging, choice of systemic regimen, and surveillance.  
• Vascular and biliary involvement of the liver lesions – decisive for confirming that a safe margin can be achieved without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
• Detailed arterial anatomy and presence of capsular infiltration – required to plan the extent of hepatic resection and to anticipate need for vascular reconstruction.  
• Brain imaging results – although extra‑hepatic disease is otherwise absent, a missing assessment of cerebral metastasis could alter the overall treatment intent.  
These missing items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, history of segmental VI-VII resection. Liver MRI: new lesion segment III (2.4 cm) and micronodule segment II. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous contralateral recurrence, possible minimally invasive approach depending on remnant volume.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the two left‑lateral lesions (segments II and III) are technically amenable to resection, but decisive information is missing. A thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) is required to exclude extra‑hepatic disease, and an accurate future liver remnant (FLR) ratio calculation is needed to confirm that the remaining liver after a left lateral sectionectomy (in the setting of a prior segmental VI‑VII resection) will be sufficient. Until these data are obtained, surgery cannot be planned safely.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain comprehensive staging: contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to evaluate vascular contact, biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR volume.  
- Measure serum CEA and document status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or pending).  
- If staging confirms absence of extra‑hepatic disease and FLR ≥30 % (≥20 % in patients with chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery: minimally invasive left lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) with parenchymal‑sparing technique, preserving segment IV and the previously resected right posterior sector. Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the micronodule in segment II and to assess margins.  
- If FLR is borderline, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left medial sector (segment IV) before resection.  
- In parallel, initiate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑4 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) given the metachronous nature of the disease and to treat any occult micrometastases. Adjust the sequence based on FLR assessment: neoadjuvant chemotherapy first if FLR is adequate, or PVE followed by chemotherapy if hypertrophy is needed.  
- Post‑operative follow‑up with serial CEA and imaging at 3‑month intervals; consider adjuvant chemotherapy if pathology shows high‑risk features (poor differentiation, vascular invasion, etc.).

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, or brain metastases.  
- Quantitative FLR ratio and detailed volumetric analysis of the remnant liver.  
- Detailed vascular anatomy and any tumor‑vessel contact in segments II‑III.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. pending) and current CEA level.  
- History of systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, response). These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, operated two years earlier with a left hepatectomy.Liver MRI: recurrence segment VIII (3.1 cm) in contact with the middle hepatic vein. CEA 200 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Isolated complex recurrence of the hepatic dome, technical assessment required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a solitary 3.1 cm recurrence in segment VIII with contact to the middle hepatic vein after a previous left hepatectomy. A parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy is technically feasible, but decisive information is missing: (a) quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) ratio/volumetry to confirm that removal of segment VIII will leave an adequate liver volume, and (b) a complete extra‑hepatic staging work‑up (chest/abdomen CT or PET) to exclude occult disease. Without these data the operation cannot be scheduled outright, but there is no absolute anatomic or oncologic contraindication.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• 1. Complete staging: obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases that were not reported.  
• 2. Liver volumetry: perform CT‑based or MRI‑based volumetric analysis to calculate the FLR. Target FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
• 3. If FLR is adequate and no extra‑hepatic disease is found, proceed to curative‑intent surgery: a laparoscopic or open segment VIII anatomical resection with en‑bloc removal of the involved portion of the middle hepatic vein; reconstruct the vein if necessary (patch or interposition graft).  
• 4. If FLR is borderline (<30 % or <40 % with prior chemotherapy), consider pre‑operative portal vein embolisation of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the remaining left liver (recognizing that left liver was resected, this step may be limited) or evaluate alternative parenchymal‑sparing techniques (e.g., wedge resection with vascular control).  
• 5. After resection, obtain pathology including KRAS/NRAS/BRAF status and microsatellite instability. Based on molecular phenotype, initiate adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab for RAS‑wildtype, or appropriate regimen for RAS‑mutant/BRAF‑mutant disease).  
• 6. Post‑operative surveillance: serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Quantitative FLR ratio/volumetry (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio).  
• Full extra‑hepatic staging results (ThoracoCTScanPerformed, AbdomenCTScanPerformed, PET‑CT).  
• Detailed vascular anatomy of the right liver (ArterialAnatomy, PortalAnatomy) to plan vein resection/reconstruction.  
• Molecular phenotype of the primary colorectal tumor (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF, MSI status).  
• History of systemic chemotherapy (type, duration, response) to assess liver parenchymal quality and need for a higher FLR threshold.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The liver lesion is solitary (1 lesion, 3.9 cm) in segment VII, isolated on thoraco‑abdominal CT and MRI, and the MDT notes it is “anatomically approachable.”  
- Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V has already removed a substantial portion of hepatic parenchyma; therefore the adequacy of the future liver remnant (FLR) after a second resection is a decisive factor. The structured analysis lists FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing, which prevents a definitive “Resectable upfront” classification.  
- Additional decisive missing items are the presence of vascular contact/invasion and detailed liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin). Because these key pieces of information are absent, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending their clarification.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain volumetric liver CT or MRI to calculate the FLR ratio after a planned segmentectomy of VII.  
   - Perform liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and an ICG clearance test to assess functional reserve.  
   - Review the hepatic arterial and portal venous anatomy with contrast‑enhanced imaging to rule out vascular invasion.  
   - Verify the status of the colorectal primary (has it been resected? if not, plan for primary tumor resection).  
   - Consider brain MRI if any neurologic symptoms are present, given the missing brain metastasis data.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if FLR is adequate or after portal vein embolisation)  
   - Because the tumor is KRAS‑mutated, initiate a standard oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months. This addresses potential micrometastatic disease and provides a window to assess tumor biology.  

3. Portal vein embolisation (PVE) if needed  
   - If volumetry shows an FLR < 30 % (normal liver) or < 40 % (post‑chemotherapy liver), perform right‑posterior PVE to hypertrophy the remnant before resection.  

4. Surgical resection  
   - Once an adequate FLR and clear vascular anatomy are confirmed, proceed with a formal segmentectomy of VII (or non‑anatomical wedge if margins allow) using intra‑operative ultrasound to ensure ≥1 cm oncologic margins.  
   - Preserve as much functional parenchyma as possible given the prior IV‑V resection.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy) as adjuvant treatment.  
   - Monitor CEA and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – essential to confirm that a second hepatic resection will leave sufficient functional liver.  
- Detailed hepatic vascular involvement (relationship of the lesion to hepatic veins, portal vein, hepatic artery).  
- Liver function assessment (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance) to gauge functional reserve.  
- Status of the colorectal primary tumor (has it been resected? location, pathology).  
- Timing of the liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) to refine prognosis and systemic therapy planning.  
- CEA level – baseline tumor marker for follow‑up.  
- Brain imaging – to definitively exclude occult cerebral metastasis, given the “Missing” entry for extra‑hepatic brain involvement.  

These missing elements must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MRI shows multiple 1‑2 cm lesions confined to segment III after a previous right hepatectomy, but the future liver remnant (FLR) required after a segment III resection is unknown (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing). Moreover, no thoraco‑abdominal CT has been performed to exclude extra‑hepatic disease (ThoracoCTScanPerformed = False, AbdomenCTScanPerformed = False). Because adequate FLR and absence of extra‑hepatic metastases are decisive for a safe hepatic resection, these pieces of information must be obtained or a pre‑operative strategy (e.g., systemic therapy, portal vein embolization) must be applied before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Obtain staging thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or osseous metastases.  
• Perform liver volumetry (CT‑ or MRI‑based) to calculate the FLR; assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin).  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab; consider anti‑EGFR therapy because RAS is wild‑type, pending primary tumor location).  
• Re‑image after 2–3 months of systemic therapy (MRI of liver, repeat CT of chest/abdomen).  
   – If disease remains limited to segment III, FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if liver is steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured) and no extra‑hepatic sites are identified, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery: an anatomic segment III resection or non‑anatomic wedge resection with negative margins, preserving segment II.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization of the segment III portal branch (or left portal branch) to hypertrophy segment II, followed by delayed segmentectomy.  
   – If multiple lesions in segment III preclude an adequate margin or FLR, consider percutaneous ablative therapies (RFA or microwave) as a liver‑sparing alternative after systemic disease control.  
• After hepatic control, evaluate the primary colorectal tumor (if still present) and treat according to standard guidelines (resection if resectable, or continue systemic therapy).  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Exact location and resection status of the primary colorectal tumor (needed to decide on anti‑EGFR use and to plan any synchronous or staged colorectal surgery).  
• Number of hepatic metastases and presence of vascular or biliary involvement (affects feasibility of a margin‑negative resection).  
• Quantitative FLR ratio/volumetry and baseline liver function (determines whether a segmentectomy is safe).  
• Results of thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Prior systemic therapy history (whether the patient has already received chemotherapy and response status).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple metachronous nodules (1–2 cm) in segment III after a prior right hepatectomy, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although confined to the left lateral section, the multifocal pattern in the only remaining liver raises concern for achieving complete clearance while preserving adequate functional parenchyma. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior major hepatectomy, this situation is considered potentially unresectable, but requires careful balance between parenchymal preservation and oncologic completeness.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define the exact number, distribution, and vascular/biliary relationships of the nodules.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and assess inflow/outflow preservation.
• Given the high CEA level (550 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA (550 ng/mL), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status) may be considered to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing)
• Given the small size and multiplicity of nodules in segment III, a combined approach is appropriate:
– Parenchymal-sparing wedge/limited resections for accessible lesions.
– Thermo-ablation (microwave/RFA) for deep or multiple small nodules to preserve parenchyma.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the lesions.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The case contains several decisive gaps that prevent an upfront determination of operability. Critical information that is missing includes (a) detailed hepatic anatomy – which segments are involved, presence of vascular or biliary contact, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio; (b) liver‑specific imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI) to confirm lesion number, size and resectability; (c) pulmonary lesion characteristics – exact size, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and functional pulmonary reserve; (d) confirmation that the pulmonary nodules are true metastases (FDG‑PET) and not benign; (e) status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms. Because these data are required to plan a safe, margin‑negative resection of both liver and lung disease, the lesions are considered potentially resectable pending completion of these assessments and neoadjuvant systemic therapy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic induction therapy – initiate a KRAS‑mutated regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to down‑size hepatic and pulmonary lesions and to assess tumor biology.  
2. Diagnostic completion – after the initial chemotherapy cycles obtain:  
   • Gadoxetate‑enhanced liver MRI (including vascular mapping) to define segmental involvement, vascular contact, and calculate FLR.  
   • High‑resolution chest CT with volumetric analysis and, if available, FDG‑PET to confirm pulmonary nodules as metastases and to evaluate mediastinal/hilar nodes.  
   • Colonoscopy or repeat abdominal imaging to verify status of the primary tumor; if not yet resected and symptomatic, schedule primary colectomy (either before or after systemic therapy depending on symptomatology).  
3. Re‑assessment – multidisciplinary review of imaging response:  
   • If liver lesions have responded and an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy) can be achieved, plan hepatic resection. Consider portal vein embolization if FLR is borderline.  
   • If pulmonary nodules are ≤5 cm, peripheral, and limited in number, evaluate for pulmonary metastasectomy; assess pulmonary function tests to ensure postoperative reserve.  
4. Surgical sequencing – preferred approach is staged resection:  
   • First, curative‑intent liver resection (major or minor depending on segmental distribution).  
   • After hepatic recovery (4–6 weeks), proceed to pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge resection or segmentectomy) if still resectable.  
   • Simultaneous liver‑lung resection may be considered only in highly selected patients with excellent performance status and limited disease burden.  
5. Adjuvant therapy – resume or continue systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively for a total of 6 months (or longer per response) and consider maintenance bevacizumab if tolerated.  
6. Surveillance – serial CEA measurements and cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most critical missing items that must be obtained before finalizing the plan are:  

- Hepatic segment(s) involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy (to calculate FLR and determine need for portal vein embolization).  
- Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI results.  
- Exact size and anatomic relationship of the bilateral pulmonary nodules, plus pulmonary function test results.  
- FDG‑PET scan to confirm pulmonary lesions as metastatic disease and to rule out additional occult sites.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or pending) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic relevance).  

Acquisition of these data will allow conversion of the “potentially resectable” classification to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the presence of nodular peritoneal disease precludes an upfront curative liver‑only operation, but resectability cannot be excluded because critical information is missing. Specifically, the peritoneal cancer index (PCI), extent of hepatic segment involvement, vascular contact, future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected are all decisive for planning a combined liver‑plus‑peritoneal cytoreductive approach. Until these data are obtained, the case remains potentially resectable after appropriate down‑staging and further staging work‑up.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain the missing staging information:  
  • Perform a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define segmental distribution, vascular involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
  • Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy or dedicated CT‑based assessment to determine PCI, sites of peritoneal involvement (including hepatoduodenal and hilar ligaments), and to obtain peritoneal biopsies for histology.  
  • Complete molecular profiling of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) and record tumor grade.  
  • Verify whether the right‑colon primary has been resected; if not, schedule a right hemicolectomy (either before or after systemic therapy depending on symptomatology).  
- Initiate systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR agent based on RAS/BRAF status) for 2–3 months with the goal of downsizing liver lesions and peritoneal implants.  
- Re‑stage with repeat CT/MRI and, if indicated, repeat diagnostic laparoscopy after chemotherapy to reassess liver disease (number, size, vascular contact, FLR) and peritoneal disease (PCI).  
- Decision algorithm after restaging:  
  • If liver disease is limited to ≤5 lesions amenable to R0 resection, FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury suspected), and PCI ≤10–12 with no involvement of critical ligaments, proceed to combined curative surgery: right hemicolectomy (if not already done) + anatomical liver resection (or parenchymal‑sparing resections) + cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC.  
  • If disease remains extensive (high PCI, unresectable vascular involvement, insufficient FLR), continue systemic therapy and consider conversion strategies (e.g., portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy) or transition to best‑supportive care.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trend and assess for treatment‑related toxicity; adjust regimen accordingly.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Molecular phenotype (RAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Status of primary tumor resection (already resected or still in situ).  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatible with safe resection.  
- Liver MRI findings (to complement CT).  
- Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) and specific sites of peritoneal involvement (including hilar/hepatoduodenal ligaments).  
- Timing of liver and peritoneal metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
- FDG‑PET scan results (to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

The patient presents with four liver metastases (1.5–3.8 cm) associated with nodular peritoneal involvement on CT. The presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. According to oncologic criteria, this situation is considered potentially resectable after a major conversion.

A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (950 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.
• The goal is to evaluate tumor biology and potential response at both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The case cannot be declared resectable upfront because decisive information is lacking. Specifically, the size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of the five bilobar liver lesions, the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and the resectability of the right‑lung metastasis are not provided. Moreover, the primary rectal tumor has not yet been addressed (resection status, need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy). These missing data require neoadjuvant systemic therapy and further imaging before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type, synchronous metastatic disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + cetuximab).  
• After 2–3 months, restage with high‑resolution liver MRI, PET‑CT, and repeat chest CT to:  
    – Determine response of liver lesions, exact size, segmental involvement, and any vascular/biliary contact.  
    – Calculate FLR ratio and decide if portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy is needed.  
    – Assess the right‑lung nodule for size, location relative to vessels/bronchi and resectability.  
• If imaging shows that all liver lesions can be cleared with an adequate FLR (≥20 % in a normal liver, ≥30 % after chemotherapy), plan a combined or staged surgical approach:  
    – Primary rectal cancer: proceed with total mesorectal excision; if the tumor remains T3 with threatened margin, give neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before resection.  
    – Liver: perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy of all five lesions; if FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization first or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
    – Lung: if the solitary right‑lung metastasis is technically resectable, schedule pulmonary metastasectomy (segmentectomy or wedge) either synchronously with liver surgery (if patient fitness permits) or in a staged fashion after hepatic resection. If not surgically resectable, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: continue systemic treatment (e.g., maintenance bevacizumab or anti‑EGFR) and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Exact size, segmental location and vascular/biliary involvement of each liver metastasis.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ratio to total liver.  
- Resectability assessment of the right‑lung metastasis (size, lobar distribution, relation to bronchi/vessels).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (has it been resected? need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy?).  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Confirmation of systemic therapy already given (if any) and response assessment.  
- PET‑CT results to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

These pieces of information are required to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases and a single right lung metastasis in the setting of a mid-rectal T3N1 tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not contraindicate a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections provided adequate future liver remnant is preserved. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.

• Given the high CEA level (330 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of six hepatic metastases and a metastatic lymph node in the hepatic pedicle indicates a high tumor burden, but resectability cannot be confirmed because decisive information is missing. Specifically, the size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of the liver lesions, the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected are all absent. Additionally, a PET‑CT to confirm that the extra‑hepatic lymph node is the only site of disease is lacking. These gaps preclude an upfront decision for surgery; they must be resolved or addressed (e.g., by downsizing chemotherapy) before a definitive operative plan can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) given KRAS mutation, high CEA and extensive hepatic disease.  
- Perform baseline staging with a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and a whole‑body FDG‑PET/CT to define lesion size, hepatic segmental involvement, vascular contact, FLR volume and to confirm that the hepatic‑pedicle node is the sole extra‑hepatic site.  
- Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months of chemotherapy with repeat imaging (MRI + PET/CT). Assess radiologic response, FLR adequacy, and nodal status.  
- If sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) are achieved, plan a staged approach:  
   • First, resect the primary left‑colon tumor (if not already removed) with standard oncologic margins.  
   • Second, perform hepatic resection of all metastases aiming for R0 margins, combined with lymphadenectomy of the hepatic‑pedicle node.  
   • If FLR is borderline, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) before hepatic resection.  
- If disease progresses or extra‑hepatic disease is found beyond the pedicle node, shift to systemic therapy alone or consider palliative measures.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Status of primary colorectal tumor resection (has it been removed?).  
- Detailed size, segmental location and vascular/biliary involvement of each liver metastasis.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Results of a whole‑body FDG‑PET/CT to confirm isolated extra‑hepatic lymph node disease.  
- Information on any prior systemic therapy and its response.  
- Specific characteristics of the hepatic‑pedicle lymph node (size, morphology, vascular relationships).  

These missing elements are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases associated with lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle. The presence of extrahepatic nodal disease at the hepatic hilum reflects systemic dissemination and markedly unfavorable tumor biology. Even if the liver lesions were technically resectable, the oncologic context precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable from a hepatobiliary perspective.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions and other para-aortic enlarged lymph nodes and a chest CT scan
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (780 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab;
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and abdominal CT after 2–3 months to reassess liver disease and nodal involvement.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (highly exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in case of major response with major regression of nodal disease and significant downsizing of liver lesions.
• Any surgical strategy would remain highly selected and dependent on sustained disease control.

E. Surgical management of liver metastases (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections or ablation guided by intra-operative ultrasound:

Response:

Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a single cerebellar metastasis that requires immediate neurosurgical or radiosurgical treatment, and multiple bilobar liver metastases of unknown number, size, segmental distribution and vascular involvement. The absence of detailed hepatic imaging, FLR assessment, and information on prior systemic therapy prevents a definitive upfront resection plan. Therefore resection of the colon primary and liver disease can only be considered after (a) control of the brain lesion and (b) down‑staging of the liver metastases with systemic therapy and completion of the missing anatomic data.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1️⃣ Neurological priority:  
   • Obtain brain MRI (if not already done) to define lesion size, edema, mass effect.  
   • Initiate steroids if edema present.  
   • Proceed with stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or microsurgical resection of the cerebellar metastasis, depending on size and accessibility.  

- 2️⃣ Systemic therapy (concurrent with or immediately after brain treatment):  
   • Start intensive first‑line chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) while awaiting molecular profiling (RAS, BRAF, MSI).  
   • Re‑evaluate CEA trend after 2–3 cycles.  

- 3️⃣ Restaging and hepatic assessment (after 2–3 months of chemotherapy):  
   • Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT‑based volumetry.  
   • Calculate future liver remnant (FLR) ratio; consider portal vein embolization if FLR <30 % (or <40 % in a cirrhotic liver).  

- 4️⃣ Surgical sequencing (if restaging shows sufficient response and resectability):  
   • Option A – “Colon first” approach: right hemicolectomy with primary tumor removal, followed by staged hepatic resection after recovery.  
   • Option B – “Combined” approach: simultaneous right hemicolectomy and liver resection if FLR adequate and operative risk acceptable.  
   • Option C – “Liver first” (rare) only if primary tumor is asymptomatic and liver disease is borderline resectable after down‑staging.  

- 5️⃣ Post‑operative adjuvant therapy:  
   • Continue systemic chemotherapy to complete a total of 6–8 cycles, adapting to molecular results (e.g., adding anti‑EGFR agents for RAS‑wild type, immunotherapy for MSI‑high).  

- 6️⃣ Ongoing surveillance:  
   • Serial CEA measurements, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis every 3 months, and brain MRI as indicated.

- Grade of differentiation and molecular phenotype (RAS, BRAF, MSI) of the primary tumor – essential for selecting targeted or immunologic agents.  
- Confirmation whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected and any obstructive/perforation symptoms – determines urgency of colon surgery.

- Results of thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI, and FLR ratio – required to plan the extent of liver resection.  
- Information on any systemic therapy already administered – influences timing of further chemotherapy and surgical windows.  
- Precise size, edema, and mass effect of the cerebellar lesion, and whether FDG‑PET or amino‑acid PET has been performed – guides neurosurgical vs. radiosurgical decision and confirms solitary brain disease.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, rectosigmoid tumor, four liver metastases and pelvic peritoneal implants at the abdominal CT scan. BRAF wild-type, CEA 320 ng/mL.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient has four liver metastases of unknown size, segmental distribution, and vascular or biliary involvement, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio is not reported. In addition, there are pelvic peritoneal implants whose extent (PCI) is unknown. Because these critical anatomic and functional parameters are missing, definitive determination of curative resection cannot be made at this time. Moreover, the primary rectosigmoid lesion has not yet been resected and its symptom status (obstruction, bleeding) is unknown. Therefore resection will require (a) systemic down‑staging chemotherapy and (b) completion of staging imaging (liver MRI, chest CT, PET‑CT, diagnostic laparoscopy) to define the liver burden, FLR adequacy, and peritoneal disease burden before any surgical plan can be finalized.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody, given BRAF wild‑type and assuming RAS wild‑type) for 2–3 months.  
2. Perform restaging work‑up after initial chemotherapy:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase to define number, size, segmental location, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR.  
   • Full thoraco‑abdominal CT and FDG‑PET/CT to assess pulmonary, nodal, and possible brain metastases.  
   • Diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal cancer index (PCI) scoring to quantify pelvic peritoneal disease and to obtain peritoneal biopsies.  
3. Re‑evaluate resectability based on restaging results:  
   • If liver disease is limited to ≤3‑4 lesions amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resections with adequate FLR (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy), plan staged or simultaneous liver resection.  
   • If peritoneal disease is limited (PCI ≤10) and no other extra‑hepatic sites are present, consider cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) combined with liver resection, either in a single operation (if technically feasible) or in a sequential approach (primary colon resection → liver resection → CRS/HIPEC).  
   • If primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) or at high risk, perform low anterior resection (or sigmoidectomy) before or concurrently with liver surgery, depending on operative risk and disease distribution.  
4. If restaging shows progression of liver or peritoneal disease, or FLR is insufficient, continue systemic therapy and consider conversion strategies (e.g., portal vein embolization) or shift to a palliative intent.  
5. Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trend; a marked decline supports response, whereas rising levels prompt earlier imaging.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Primary tumor status: whether it has already been resected and presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameters, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetry.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and any prior systemic therapy.  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging: thoracic CT, FDG‑PET/CT, brain imaging.  
- Peritoneal disease burden: Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) and morphology of pelvic implants.  

These items must be obtained to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

The MDT already judged “not resectable upfront,” indicating that a prerequisite (effective down‑staging chemotherapy and complete staging work‑up) is required before any surgical attempt.

- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type.

   • Response of liver lesions, number of viable metastases, vascular/biliary involvement, and FLR calculation.  
   • Number, size and distribution of pulmonary nodules.

   • ≤4 liver metastases confined to segments that allow an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), and no major vascular invasion, and

- If restaging shows persistent extensive bilobar disease, inadequate FLR, or diffuse pulmonary involvement, continue systemic therapy (maintenance biologic ± fluoropyrimidine) and reassess for further conversion attempts or enrolment in a clinical trial.

- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement, size of each metastasis, and presence of vascular or biliary invasion.

- Timing of metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and prior systemic therapy exposure.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the presence of a solitary right‑iliac bone metastasis and multiple liver lesions in segments IV, V and VIII precludes immediate curative surgery. Definitive resectability cannot be judged until (a) systemic chemotherapy is delivered and response assessed, (b) the primary colon tumor is either resected or proven resectable, (c) detailed liver imaging (MRI) defines the number, size and vascular relationship of the hepatic lesions, and (d) an FLR volume calculation is performed. These prerequisite actions are essential to determine whether a liver‑first, colon‑first, or combined approach can be pursued.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated left‑sided colon cancer (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFOXIRI with bevacizumab).  
- Concurrently obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI, a thoraco‑abdominal CT (including chest) and a bone scan or PET‑CT to fully stage extra‑hepatic disease and to characterize the iliac lesion (lytic vs blastic, fracture risk).  
- Evaluate the primary tumor for obstruction, perforation or bleeding; if symptomatic or technically resectable, schedule a colon resection (segmental colectomy) either before or after the first cycle of chemotherapy, depending on symptom burden.  
- After 2–3 months of systemic therapy, restage with repeat imaging; calculate future liver remnant (FLR) using volumetry.  
- If liver disease has responded to ≤4 lesions, no major vascular invasion, and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if underlying liver disease), plan curative intent liver resection (e.g., anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing resections of segments IV, V, VIII).  
- For the solitary iliac bone metastasis, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy or surgical fixation if fracture risk is high; systemic therapy will also address the bone lesion.  
- If restaging shows progression or unresectable liver disease, continue systemic therapy and consider palliative local measures (radiofrequency ablation, hepatic arterial therapy, bone radiotherapy).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Primary tumor status (resected or not, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Number, maximal diameter and vascular/biliary involvement of liver metastases.  
- FLR volumetric assessment.  
- Results of thoracic imaging to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Detailed characterization of the iliac bone lesion (lytic vs blastic, fracture risk, epidural extension).  
- Baseline CEA level and timing (synchronous vs metachronous) of liver and bone metastases.  
- Confirmation of whether any systemic therapy has already been administered.  

These items are critical to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable  
• Reasoning: The patient has limited hepatic disease (2 lesions) and a solitary left‑lung nodule, which in principle can be removed surgically together with the rectal primary. However, key anatomic information is missing (size, segmental distribution, vascular contact of liver lesions; FLR ratio; detailed pulmonary nodule characteristics) and the primary tumor has not yet been resected or staged for neoadjuvant radiotherapy. Moreover, no systemic therapy has been administered to assess tumor biology and response. Because a specific prerequisite (completion of systemic chemotherapy ± radiotherapy and completion of definitive imaging) is required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, the case is “Potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT):  
   – Systemic chemotherapy appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type rectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody).  
   – Concurrent or sequential short‑course radiotherapy / long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary, based on tumor height and sphincter considerations.  
• Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of TNT:  
   – Liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion size, segmental location, vascular involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
   – FDG‑PET/CT to confirm metabolic activity of the pulmonary nodule, exclude additional extra‑hepatic sites, and assess for occult bone or brain disease.  
   – High‑resolution chest CT to detail the pulmonary nodule’s relationship to bronchi and vessels.  
• If restaging shows favorable response and all lesions remain resectable:  
   – Plan a staged or simultaneous surgical approach, depending on patient fitness and operative risk.  
   – First, address the rectal primary (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) after completion of neoadjuvant radiotherapy.  
   – Second, perform parenchyma‑sparing liver resection of the two metastases, ensuring an FLR ≥20 % (≥30 % if steatosis/cirrhosis). If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization before liver surgery.  
   – Third, perform pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge resection or segmentectomy) of the left lung nodule, either in the same operative session (if technically feasible) or as a separate staged procedure.  
• Post‑operative management:  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy to complete the planned total duration (typically 6 months total).  
   – Consider maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy given RAS‑wild‑type status, especially if residual disease is present.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance (CT/MRI every 3–6 months) for early detection of recurrence.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Primary tumor status: whether the rectal cancer has already been resected and the need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy.  
• Histologic grade of differentiation of the rectal primary.  
• Detailed liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameters, hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, arterial anatomy, and FLR ratio.  
• Confirmation that a liver MRI has been performed.  
• Information on any systemic chemotherapy already given.  
• Full characterization of the pulmonary nodule: size, exact lobar location, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and FDG‑PET uptake.  
• Results of FDG‑PET/CT for whole‑body staging (including brain).  
These missing items are essential to confirm resectability, plan the extent of hepatic and pulmonary surgery, and determine the need for pre‑operative portal vein embolization or additional systemic therapy.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Not resectable  
Reasoning: The case describes eight bilobar liver metastases together with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis on abdominal CT. Bilobar disease of this volume, in the presence of peritoneal spread, exceeds the anatomical and oncological limits for curative liver resection or combined cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC. No information is provided that would suggest the peritoneal disease is limited enough to permit complete cytoreduction, nor that the liver lesions are amenable to a limited‑resection strategy with an adequate future liver remnant. Consequently, curative‑intent surgery is excluded at this stage.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Obtain full molecular profiling of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H status) and histologic grade; these results will guide targeted agents and immunotherapy.  
- Perform a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to confirm the absence of pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease beyond the known peritoneal implants.  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with a modern doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with biologic therapy selected according to the molecular profile (anti‑VEGF if RAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR if RAS‑wild type, pembrolizumab if MSI‑high).  
- Monitor response with interval imaging (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI preferred for lesion measurement) after 2–3 months of therapy.  
- Re‑assess resectability after systemic treatment: if there is a marked radiologic response with reduction of liver tumor burden to ≤4 lesions confined to ≤2 contiguous segments and peritoneal disease regresses to a low Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI ≤10), consider conversion to staged liver resection followed by cytoreductive surgery + HIPEC.  
- If the primary tumor remains in situ and becomes symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation), address it promptly with either endoscopic stenting or surgical resection, preferably after initial systemic control.  
- Throughout treatment, provide supportive care, nutritional optimization, and discuss clinical‑trial enrollment for conversion‑therapy protocols or novel systemic agents.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) – essential for selecting targeted systemic therapy.  
- Histologic grade of differentiation – influences prognosis and aggressiveness of treatment.  
- Status of primary tumor resection and presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms – determines need for urgent primary‑site surgery.  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics (size of each metastasis, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion) and FLR ratio – required to evaluate any future liver‑sparing approach.  
- Comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal imaging (including PET‑CT) – needed to rule out additional extra‑hepatic sites that would further preclude surgery.  
- Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) and specific peritoneal sites involved – critical to decide whether cytoreductive surgery + HIPEC could ever be feasible.  
These missing items are the most decisive for refining the treatment plan and any future consideration of surgical intervention.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT notes that the liver disease is technically resectable, but several decisive elements are missing or pending. The primary colon tumor has not been confirmed as resected, the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio is unknown, and comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude extra‑hepatic disease has not been documented. Moreover, the presence of vascular contact (segment VIII lesion with the middle hepatic vein) and a markedly elevated CEA (1150 ng/mL) indicate a high systemic burden that traditionally warrants neoadjuvant systemic therapy before any definitive surgery. Because a specific prerequisite (completion of systemic chemotherapy and full staging including FLR assessment) must be fulfilled, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain complete staging: perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases that are currently listed as Missing.  
- Assess hepatic functional reserve: calculate FLR using volumetric CT or MRI; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), plan portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy.  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated, BRAF‑wild‑type disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab). Deliver 2–3 months of treatment with imaging reassessment after each cycle.  
- Re‑image liver (MRI with hepatobiliary contrast) to evaluate response of the five lesions, particularly the segment VIII lesion’s relationship to the middle hepatic vein, and to confirm that vascular involvement remains resectable.  
- If the primary colon tumor remains in situ and is not obstructing, schedule a simultaneous or staged colon resection after systemic therapy, preferring a staged approach if liver surgery is extensive.  
- Once systemic disease is controlled, FLR is adequate, and no extra‑hepatic disease is identified, proceed to parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (e.g., anatomical or non‑anatomical resections preserving the middle hepatic vein or using vein reconstruction if needed).  
- Post‑operative management: resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy as adjuvant therapy, monitor CEA trend, and schedule regular imaging surveillance.

Step 3 - Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. pending).  
- Presence or absence of obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms from the primary lesion.  
- Comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal imaging results (CT or PET‑CT) to confirm lack of extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volumetric assessment and compatibility with planned resection.  
- Details of arterial anatomy and extent of vascular contact/invasion beyond the noted middle hepatic vein involvement.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
- Information on biliary, portal or other hepatic structure involvement that could affect resectability.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is potentially resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the three lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. a chest CT scan
